title: Infrastructure as Code Security
summary: Infrastructure as code security is the practice of treating the definition files that create servers, networks, identities and storage as reviewable, testable artefacts and of enforcing security requirements on them before anything is deployed. Instead of clicking through a console, teams describe their desired infrastructure in files, commit them to version control, and let an automation pipeline apply them. That shift moves security left: a misconfiguration is now a line of text in a merge request, so it can be caught by a diff review, a static analyser, a policy engine or a secret scanner long before it reaches production. The mechanism matters because the file is the source of truth, so one mistake is reproduced faithfully in every environment it is applied to. The usual mistake is treating the scanner as the whole control and ignoring drift, which is any change made outside the pipeline that the files no longer describe. Security here also covers the pipeline itself, since whoever can merge to the main branch can effectively redefine the whole estate.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-218: Secure Software Development Framework

beginner.definition: Infrastructure as code means describing your servers, networks and storage in text files instead of clicking buttons in a control panel. The automation tool reads those files and builds the real environment for you. Infrastructure as code security means checking those files for safety problems before they are used. It is also called IaC security, where IaC stands for infrastructure as code.
beginner.whyItMatters: A wrong click usually affects one system, and you can fix it by hand. A wrong line in an infrastructure file can be copied into hundreds of systems at once. That is how a storage bucket becomes public or a database loses its password protection. Reviewing the file is much cheaper than repairing a live environment. This approach also keeps a written record of who changed what and when.
howItWorks: Engineers write the wanted setup, such as networks and servers, in plain text files.
The files are stored in a version control system, which records every change and who made it.
A colleague reviews the change and can question anything that looks risky before it is approved.
An automated scanner checks the file for known problems, such as open ports or missing encryption.
A policy tool blocks changes that break company rules, for example giving everyone administrator rights.
The pipeline then builds the environment, and any manual change afterwards is called drift.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared flat where every repair follows a written list on the fridge. The list says which keys open which door and how the boiler is set. If someone adds one line saying the front door is always unlocked, the problem repeats for every new tenant who follows the list. So the flatmates read every new line together before it takes effect. If one person later changes the boiler by hand, the fridge list becomes wrong, and nobody knows the real state of the flat. Infrastructure as code security is that careful reading, plus noticing when the list no longer matches reality.
takeaways: A configuration file can create many systems, so a small mistake has a very large effect.
Check the files before deployment, not only after the systems are running.
Watch for drift, which means changes made by hand outside the pipeline.

objectives: Explain what infrastructure as code means and why the definition files become the source of truth.
Describe how security checks such as reviewing, scanning and policy enforcement fit into a deployment pipeline.
Give examples of common infrastructure misconfigurations, including public storage and overbroad roles.
Explain what configuration drift is and why it undermines the guarantees of a review process.
Justify why the automation pipeline itself must be protected as a high value asset.
